concepts.title: Continuous and Discrete Signals
concepts.one_liner: Continuous signals exist in nature as infinite functions, while discrete signals are finite sequences of numbers sampled for computer processing.
concepts.content: Most signals that exist in nature are infinite continuous signals. When these signals are introduced into a computer, they are sampled and transformed into a finite sequence of numbers, which is referred to as a discrete signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Computers cannot process the infinite precision of natural continuous signals; they must be converted into discrete numerical sequences to be stored and manipulated digitally.
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous signals are infinite functions of a real variable found in nature.

concepts.title: Sampling Equation
concepts.one_liner: The sampling equation $\ell[n] = \ell(n \Delta T)$ relates a continuous signal to its discrete sequence via a sampling period $\Delta T$.
concepts.content:
If we consider the light that reaches one camera photo sensor, we could write it as a one dimensional function of time, $\ell(t)$, where $\ell(t)$ denotes the incident light at time $t$, and $t$ is a continuous variable that can take on any real value. The signal $\ell(t)$ is then sampled in time (as is done in a video) by the camera where the values are only captured at discrete times (e.g., 30 times per second). In that case, the signal $\ell$ will be defined only on discrete time instants and we will write the sequence of measured values as $\ell[n]$, where $n$ can only take on integer values. 

The relationship between the discrete and the continuous signals is given by the sampling equation:
$$\ell[n] = \ell(n~\Delta T)$$
where $\Delta T$ is the sampling period. For instance, $\Delta T = 1/30$ s in the case of sampling the signal 30 times per second. 

As is common in signal processing, we will use parenthesis to indicate continuous variables and brackets to denote discrete variables. For instance, if we sample the signal shown in (see figure: Fig (a) A continuous signal, and (b) a discrete signal obtained by sampling the continuous signal at the times $t=n$.) (a) once every second ($\Delta T = 1$ s) we get the discrete signal shown in (see figure: Fig (a) A continuous signal, and (b) a discrete signal obtained by sampling the continuous signal at the times $t=n$.) concepts.title: Signal Extent (Infinite, Finite, Periodic)
concepts.one_liner: Signals are classified by their extent as infinite length, finite length, or periodic.
concepts.content: Both continuous and discrete signals can be classified according to their extent. Infinite length signals are signals that extend over the entire support $\ell[n]$ for $n \in (-\infty, \infty)$. Finite length signals have non-zero values on a compact time interval and they are zero outside, i.e. $\ell[n] = 0$ for $n \notin S$ where $S$ is a finite length interval. A signal $\ell[n]$ is periodic if there is a value $N$ such that $\ell[n] = \ell[n + k N]$ for all $n$ and $k$. A periodic signal is an infinite length signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Categorizing signals by their duration and repetition helps in choosing the correct mathematical tools (like sums vs. integrals) for analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Infinite length signals span the entire time axis.

concepts.title: DC Value
concepts.one_liner: The DC value represents the mean or average value of a signal.
concepts.content:
An important quantity is the mean value of a signal, often called the DC value. DC stands for direct current, a term originating from electrical engineering that is still commonly used even for signals unrelated to electricity. In the case of an image, the DC component is the average intensity of the image. 

For a finite signal of length $N$ (or a periodic signal), the DC value is:
$$\mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \ell[n]$$
If the signal is infinite, the average value is:
$$\mu = \lim_{N \xrightarrow{} \infty} \frac{1}{2N+1} \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \ell[n]$$
concepts.motivation_md: The DC value identifies the constant offset or average level of a signal, which is fundamental in both electrical circuits and image processing.

concepts.title: Signal Energy
concepts.one_liner: Signal energy is defined as the sum of the squared magnitude values of a signal.
concepts.content:
Another important quantity to characterize a signal is its energy. Following an analogy with physics, the energy of a signal is defined as the sum of squared magnitude values:
$$E = \sum_{n = -\infty}^{\infty} \left| \ell[n] \right| ^2$$

Signal energy and general physical energy are equivalent up to a normalization constant. For instance, the energy dissipated by a resistance $R$ with voltage $v(t)$ is:
\begin{equation}
E = \frac{1}{R} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} v(t) ^2 dt
\end{equation}

Signals are further classified as finite energy and infinite energy signals. Finite length signals have finite energy, while periodic signals are considered infinite energy signals when measuring energy across the entire time axis.
concepts.motivation_md: Energy provides a measure of the 'strength' or 'size' of a signal, allowing for comparisons and classification of signals based on their total magnitude over time.

concepts.title: Signal Distance Metrics
concepts.one_liner: Signal distance metrics, such as the squared Euclidean distance, are used to compare the similarity between two signals.
concepts.content:
If we want to compare two signals, we can use the squared Euclidean distance (squared L2 norm) between them:
$$D^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \left| \ell_1 [n] - \ell_2 [n] \right| ^2$$
However, the Euclidean distance (L2) is often a poor metric when comparing the actual content of two images; developing better metrics is an active area of research. Sometimes, the L2 metric is applied in a different representation space rather than directly on pixel values. 

The same definitions apply to continuous signals, where equations are analogous by replacing sums with integrals. For instance, the energy of a continuous signal is $E = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left| \ell( t ) \right|^2 dt$, assuming the integral is finite. Most natural signals will have infinite energy.
concepts.motivation_md: Quantifying the difference between signals is essential for tasks like image recognition, noise reduction, and signal comparison.

concepts.title: 1D Convolution
concepts.one_liner: The 1D convolution computes output values as a linear weighted sum of an input signal and a kernel, where weights depend on their relative positions.
concepts.content:
The convolution, denoted $\circ$, between a signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$ and the convolutional kernel $h\left[n \right]$ is defined as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =  \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[n-k \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$

The convolution computes the output values as a linear weighted sum. The weight between the input sample $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$ and the output sample $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right]$ is a function $h\left[n, k \right]$ that depends only on their relative position $n-k$. Therefore, $h\left[n, k \right]=h\left[n-k \right]$. If the signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$ has a finite length, $N$, then the sum is only done in the interval $k \in \left[0,N-1\right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution is a fundamental operation in signal processing and neural networks that allows for translation-invariant filtering. By using weights that only depend on the relative distance between input and output samples, it enables the same local pattern-matching operation to be applied consistently across an entire signal.

concepts.title: Convolution Versus Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Convolution and correlation are related operators that use the same kernel, but convolution mirrors the kernel around the origin.
concepts.content:
The convolution is related to the correlation operator. In the correlation, the weights are defined as $h\left[n, k \right]=h\left[k-n \right]$. The convolution and the correlation use the same kernel but mirrored around the origin. The correlation is also translation invariant.

Most of the literature in neural networks calls convolution to the correlation operator. As the kernels are learned, the distinction is not important most of the time.
concepts.motivation_md: While mathematically distinct due to the mirroring of the kernel, convolution and correlation perform similar tasks of measuring similarity or filtering. In deep learning, the distinction is often ignored because the network can simply learn a mirrored version of the kernel if needed.

concepts.title: Commutative Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: One important property of the convolution is that it is commutative, meaning the order of the signal and kernel can be swapped.
concepts.content:
One important property of the convolution is that it is commutative: $h\left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right] \circ h\left[n\right]$. This property is easy to prove by changing the variables, $k = n - k'$, so that:

$$h \left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[n-k \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right] = \sum_{k'=-\infty}^{\infty} h \left[k' \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-k' \right]  = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] \circ h \left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Commutativity simplifies mathematical analysis and implementation, as it allows us to treat the filter and the signal symmetrically.

concepts.title: Convolution Procedure
concepts.one_liner: The convolution procedure involves mirroring the kernel, shifting it to a target location, and calculating a weighted sum of the surrounding input values.
concepts.content: The convolution operation can be described in words as: first take the kernel $h\left[k\right]$ and mirror it $h\left[-k \right]$, then shift the mirrored kernel so that the origin is at location $n$, then multiply the input values around location $n$ by the mirrored kernel and sum the result. Store the result in the output vector $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right]$. For instance, if the convolutional kernel has three non-zero values: $h\left[-1 \right] =1$, $h\left[0 \right] = 2$ and $h\left[1 \right] = 3$, then the output value at location $n$ is $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = 3 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-1\right]+2 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] + 1 \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+1\right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the step-by-step mechanical procedure of convolution (flip, shift, multiply, sum) is essential for implementing the algorithm and for building an intuition of how kernels interact with signals.

concepts.one_liner: For finite length signals, convolution can be explicitly represented as a matrix-vector multiplication.
concepts.content:

$$\begin{bmatrix}
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 0 \right] \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 1 \right] \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 2 \right] \\
\vdots \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ N-1 \right]
\end{bmatrix}
 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  h\left[0\right] ~&~ h\left[-1\right] ~&~ 0 ~&~ ... ~&~ 0 \\
  h\left[1\right] ~&~ h\left[0\right] ~&~ h\left[-1\right] ~&~... ~&~ 0 \\

  0 ~&~ 0 ~&~ 0 ~&~... ~&~ h\left[0\right] 
 \end{bmatrix}

 \begin{bmatrix}
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[0\right] \\

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = h \left[n,m\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] =  \sum_{k,l}h \left[n-k,m-l \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k,l \right]$$

The particular kernel used in the figure averages in the vertical direction and takes differences horizontally. The output image reflects that processing, with horizontal differences accentuated and vertical changes diminished. To compute one of the pixels in the output image, we start with an input image patch of $3 \times 3$ pixels, we flip the convolutional kernel upside-down and left-right, and then we multiply all the pixels in the image patch with the corresponding flipped kernel values and we sum the results.

concepts.title: Properties of the Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolution is a linear operation characterized by properties such as commutativity, associativity, distributivity, and shift-invariance.
concepts.content:
The convolution is a linear operation that is important to be familiar with. Its properties include:

-   **Commutative**. The convolution is commutative, $h\left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right] \circ h\left[n\right]$, which means that the order of convolutions is irrelevant. This is not true for the correlation.

-   **Associative**. Convolutions can be applied in any order: $\ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_2 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right] = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]) = (\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right]) \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]$. In practice, for finite length signals, the associative property might be affected by boundary conditions.

-   **Distributive** with respect to the sum: $\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] + \ell_3\left[n\right] ) = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right] +  \ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right]$

-   **Shift**. If the input signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$ is translated by a constant $n_0$, the output is translated by the same constant: $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] =  h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right]$. Translating the kernel is equivalent.

-   **Support**. The convolution of a discrete signal of length $N$ with another of length $M$ results in a signal with length $L \leq M+N-1$.

-   **Identity**. The convolution has an identity function, the impulse $\delta \left[n\right]$, which is 1 for $n=0$ and zero elsewhere. The convolution of the impulse with any signal returns the same signal: $\delta \left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right]$.

concepts.title: Handling Boundaries in Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Implementing a convolution requires deciding how to handle image boundaries, often by padding the input to maintain the output size.
concepts.content:
When implementing a convolution, one must decide how to handle image boundaries. One solution is omitting pixels affected by the boundary, but this causes the output size to differ from the input and can result in significant data loss for large kernels.

[FIGURE:6b79adcf26f0dfd2]

Only the green region contains values that can be computed without boundary handling. The most general approach is extending the input image by adding $N$ pixels left and right and $M$ pixels at the top and bottom for a kernel with support $\left[ -N, N \right] \times \left[-M, M\right]$. Typical padding choices include:

- Zero padding: Set pixels outside the boundary to zero or another constant like the mean image value.
- Circular padding: Replicate pixels from the opposite side, transforming the signal into a periodic infinite signal: $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[(n)_P,(m)_Q\right]$.
- Mirror padding: Reflect valid image pixels over the boundary; this often yields the best results.
- Repeat padding: Set the value to that of the nearest valid output image pixel.

concepts.title: Circular Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Circular convolution is a special case of convolution that uses circular padding, treating the input signal as an infinite periodic extension.
concepts.content:
[FIGURE:adb812066d7186ad]

Circular convolution is an analytically useful technique that uses circular padding to extend a signal beyond its boundaries. The circular convolution of two signals $h$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ of length $N$ is defined as:

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] =  \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$

In this formulation, the signal $h \left[ (n)_N \right]$ is the infinite periodic extension, with period $N$, of the finite length signal $h \left[n \right]$. The output is also a periodic signal with period $N$, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[(n)_N \right]$. Circular convolution shares the same properties as standard convolution, such as commutativity.
concepts.motivation_md: Circular convolution is analytically convenient for reducing boundary artifacts and is a fundamental operation when working with periodic signals or Fourier transforms.

concepts.title: Convolution in the Continuous Domain
concepts.one_liner: Continuous convolution defines the interaction of two continuous signals by replacing the discrete sums of standard convolution with integrals.
concepts.content:
The convolution in the continuous domain is defined similarly to discrete signals but replaces sums with integrals. Given two continuous signals $h(t)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, the convolution operator is defined as:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$

The properties of continuous domain convolution are analogous to discrete convolution, with commutative, associative, and distributive relationships still holding. We can also define the impulse, $\delta (t)$, in the continuous domain such that $\ell(t) \circ \delta(t) = \ell(t)$. The impulse is zero everywhere except at the origin, where it takes an infinitely high value so that its integral is equal to 1:
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) dt = 1$$
The impulse function is also called the impulse distribution or the Dirac delta function.

The convolution in the continuous domain is defined similarly to discrete signals but replaces sums with integrals. Given two continuous signals $h(t)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, the convolution operator is defined as:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$

The properties of continuous domain convolution are analogous to discrete convolution, with commutative, associative, and distributive relationships still holding. We can also define the impulse, $\delta (t)$, in the continuous domain such that $\ell(t) \circ \delta(t) = \ell(t)$. The impulse is zero everywhere except at the origin, where it takes an infinitely high value so that its integral is equal to 1:
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) dt = 1$$
The impulse function is also called the impulse distribution or the Dirac delta function.

concepts.title: Cross-Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Cross-correlation is a translation-invariant operator used to locate templates in an image, differing from convolution by not inverting the kernel.
concepts.content:
The cross-correlation operator provides a technique to locate a template in an image and is closely related to convolution. The cross-correlation $\star$ between an image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and a kernel $h$ with square support $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$ is:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\star h =  \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$

Unlike convolution, where the kernel is inverted left-right and up-down, cross-correlation does not invert the kernel. For example, convolving an upward-pointing triangle kernel with impulses results in upward-pointing triangles, whereas cross-correlation results in downward-pointing triangles. While convolution outputs maximum values for inverted matches, cross-correlation outputs maximum values at the center of direct template matches.

concepts.title: Normalized Cross-Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Normalized cross-correlation improves template matching by normalizing the kernel and scaling the output by the local standard deviation of the image.
concepts.content:
Normalized cross-correlation at location $(n,m)$ is the dot product between a template $h$ (normalized to zero mean and unit norm) and a local image patch $p$ of the same size, also normalized to unit norm. First, the kernel $h$ is normalized to $\hat{h}$. The output is then calculated as:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \frac{1}{\sigma \left[n,m \right]} \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] \hat{h} \left[k,l \right]$$

The output is scaled by the local standard deviation $\sigma[n,m]$ of the image patch centered at $(n,m)$. The local mean $\mu[n,m]$ and variance $\sigma^2[n,m]$ are computed over the kernel's support $(2N+1)^2$. While this method can correctly detect templates like the letter 'a' in @fig-normcorr, it is fragile and only useful under limited conditions, as it is not robust to rotation, scaling, or changes in appearance like font variations.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard cross-correlation is sensitive to changes in local image brightness and contrast; normalization makes the matching process more robust to these variations.

concepts.title: Impulse Response
concepts.one_liner: The impulse response is the output of a linear time-invariant system when the input is a single impulse.
concepts.content: For a linear time-invariant (LTI) filter with kernel $h\left[n\right]$, the output from an impulse $\delta[n]$ is $y\left[n\right] = h\left[n\right]$. Similarly, the output of a translated impulse $\delta \left[n -n_0 \right]$ is $h \left[n -n_0 \right]$. Because the kernel $h\left[n\right]$ defines the system's response to an impulse, it is also called the impulse response of the system.
concepts.motivation_md: The impulse response allows us to characterize the entire behavior of a linear system by knowing only how it reacts to a single point input.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- The impulse response $h[n]$ is the kernel that defines a linear time-invariant (LTI) system.", "- Knowing the impulse response allows for the calculation of the system's output for any arbitrary input via convolution." ]
